title: Early against Late: A contrast on dark energy in the light of DESI DR2
comment: 11 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables and 2 appendices. Comments are welcome
summary: Recent findings from Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Baryon Acoustic Oscillation (BAO) measurements, combined with Type Ia supernovae and Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) data, suggest potential parameter-level deviations from $Λ\text{CDM}$. However, parameter exclusions omit prior-volume penalties, whereas Bayesian evidence uncovers a stark dichotomy between early- and late-time dynamics. To quantify this effect, we perform a Bayesian model comparison that explicitly accounts for the cosmological epoch of dark energy dynamics, contrasting two schemes acting in opposite epochs of cosmic history: pre-recombination Early Dark Energy (EDE) and late-time Chevallier--Polarski--Linder (CPL), both measured against a baseline $Λ$CDM. We validate the learned harmonic-mean estimator against \texttt{UltraNest} (at background level) before applying it to the CMB analysis. Background-only data already disfavor both extensions, yielding $\ln B_{Λ\text{CDM},\text{EDE}} = 2.45 \pm 0.25$ and $\ln B_{Λ\text{CDM},\text{CPL}} = 3.45 \pm 0.24$. Including CMB sharpens this result: EDE is decisively rejected ($\ln B_{Λ\text{CDM},\text{EDE}} = 12.44 \pm 0.05$) with its early-time fraction constrained to $10^3\,Ω_e^{\rm EDE} = 2.0^{+0.6}_{-1.0}$, whereas CPL remains moderately disfavored ($\ln B_{Λ\text{CDM},\text{CPL}} = 2.33 \pm 0.06$), even though 2D parameter posteriors for both models display a multi-$σ$ deviation from $Λ\text{CDM}$. Thus, Bayesian evidence weakens reported preferences for dark energy dynamics, with the impact depending on the cosmic epoch involved, confirmed by our functional reconstructions of $w_{\rm de}(z)$ and $Ω_{\rm de}(z)$ from posterior samples.

AI.tldr: DESI BAO data combined with Type Ia supernovae and CMB suggest parameter-level deviations from ΛCDM, but Bayesian model comparison reveals the opposite trend: EDE and late-time CPL dark energy models are disfavored relative to ΛCDM. The disfavouring is epoch-dependent, with EDE decisively rejected (lnB = 12.44) while CPL is only moderately disfavored (lnB = 2.33).
AI.motivation: Recent cosmological data hint at deviations from ΛCDM at the parameter level, but these parameter exclusions ignore prior-volume penalties. The authors aim to quantify whether such deviations survive rigorous Bayesian model comparison, and whether the epoch of dark energy dynamics (early vs. late) matters for the strength of the evidence against these extensions.
AI.method: The authors perform Bayesian model comparison contrasting pre-recombination Early Dark Energy (EDE) and late-time Chevallier-Polarski-Linder (CPL) parametrization against a baseline ΛCDM. They validate the learned harmonic-mean estimator against UltraNest at the background level before applying it to full CMB analysis, and use functional reconstructions of w_de(z) and Ω_de(z) from posterior samples.

With CMB, EDE is decisively rejected (lnB = 12.44±0.05) with early-time fraction constrained to 10^3 Ω_e^EDE = 2.0^{+0.6}_{-1.0}; CPL is moderately disfavored (lnB = 2.33±0.06), despite both models showing multi-σ deviations in 2D parameter posteriors from ΛCDM.
AI.conclusion: Bayesian evidence weakens the reported parameter-level preferences for dark energy dynamics from DESI BAO data, with the strength of disfavor depending on the cosmological epoch of the dark energy dynamics. title: Linking orbital history to the quenching of isolated dwarf galaxies
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, submitted to OJAp, comments welcome
summary: Recent discoveries of isolated dwarf galaxies (${M}_{\star}\sim 10^{7-9}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$) with no signs of ongoing star formation have challenged the prevailing notion that these solitary systems are exclusively star-forming. Investigating the origins of isolated quenched dwarfs provides important clues into the dominant processes driving galaxy quenching as a function of environment and stellar mass. In this study, we identify central dwarf galaxies in the Illustris-TNG50 cosmological simulation with ${M}_{\star} \sim 10^{7-9}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$, evaluate their star formation and orbital histories, and investigate how their dark matter halo properties correlate with quenching and interactions with massive neighbors. We find that $R_{\rm{peri}}$, defined as the closest separation ever attained between a central dwarf and a galaxy more massive than ${M}_{\star}> 10^{10}~{\rm M}_{\odot}$, is a reliable metric for inferring the star formation history of central dwarfs in TNG50. We also show that isolated quenched dwarf galaxies separate into backsplash and non-backsplash subpopulations as a function of $R_{\rm{peri}}$, and that non-backsplash galaxies are consistent with being quenched by cosmic web stripping or internal feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, we find that $R_{\rm{peri}}$ correlates strongly with dark matter halo mass and star formation proxies based on halo maximum circular velocity, which are commonly used in empirical galaxy-halo connection models. These predictions can be tested with data from upcoming deep and wide surveys (e.g., Rubin LSST and Roman) that are anticipated to significantly increase the cosmic census of dwarf galaxies.

Quenched isolated dwarfs split into backsplash and non-backsplash populations based on R_peri, with non-backsplash galaxies quenched by cosmic web stripping or internal feedback.
AI.motivation: Isolated dwarf galaxies with no ongoing star formation challenge the prevailing expectation that such solitary systems are exclusively star-forming. Understanding their origins provides crucial clues about the dominant quenching processes as a function of environment and stellar mass.
AI.method: The authors identify central dwarf galaxies (M★ ∼ 10^7-9 M⊙) in the Illustris-TNG50 cosmological simulation, evaluate their star formation and orbital histories, and investigate how dark matter halo properties correlate with quenching and interactions with massive neighbors (M★ > 10^10 M⊙).
AI.result: R_peri (minimum separation between a central dwarf and a massive galaxy) reliably predicts central dwarf star formation histories. Isolated quenched dwarfs separate into backsplash and non-backsplash subpopulations based on R_peri. R_peri also correlates strongly with dark matter halo mass and star formation proxies from halo maximum circular velocity.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide testable predictions for upcoming deep and wide surveys (e.g., Rubin LSST and Roman) that will significantly expand the cosmic census of dwarf galaxies, potentially distinguishing between quenching mechanisms such as environment-driven processes (backsplash/stripping) versus internal feedback.

title: Tracing the Cosmic Origins: Machine Learning Reconstruction of the Primordial Density Field from EoR Observations
comment: 18 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society (MNRAS)
summary: Reconstructing the initial conditions of the Universe from late-time tracers would unlock cosmological information buried by non-linear structure formation and astrophysics. We reconstruct the initial density field at $z\sim300$ from simulated 21-cm and CO(1-0) line-intensity maps at $z\sim8$ generated with LIMFAST. Using a three-dimensional U-Net, we reconstruct the initial conditions and evaluate its impact on cosmological parameter constraints. The two tracers probe complementary environments: 21-cm emission traces neutral, low-density regions of the intergalactic medium, while CO traces overdense, star-forming regions. To emulate realistic observations, we model instrumental effects for SKA1-Low- and COMAP-ERA-like surveys, including finite angular resolution and thermal noise. We assess reconstruction performance through the cross-correlation coefficient between reconstructed and true initial density fields, $|C(k)|$. In the noiseless case, combining both tracers delivers the most accurate recovery across ionisation states, with $|C(k)| \gtrsim$ 0.90 for $k \lesssim$ 0.75 Mpc$^{-1}$. With observational effects, small-scale information is degraded, but combining tracers still achieves $|C(k)| \gtrsim$ 0.70 for $k \lesssim$ 0.3 Mpc$^{-1}$. To quantify information gain, we perform simulation-based inference of cosmological parameters from power-spectrum summaries before and after reconstruction. In both noiseless and noisy settings, reconstruction tightens parameter constraints: uncertainties on $σ_8$ and $n_{\rm s}$ improve by $\sim2\times$, with smaller but consistent gains for other parameters. This is further confirmed using Kullback-Leibler divergence diagnostics for an ensemble of observations. These results indicate that joint analysis of future 21-cm and CO surveys, combined with such reconstruction, can partially recover otherwise inaccessible cosmological information.

AI.tldr: This paper reconstructs the initial density field at z~300 from simulated 21-cm and CO(1-0) line-intensity maps at z~8 using a 3D U-Net. Combining both tracers yields cross-correlation coefficients >0.90 (noiseless) and >0.70 (with observational effects) against true initial conditions. Simulation-based inference shows the reconstruction tightens cosmological parameter constraints, particularly improving σ₈ and n_s uncertainties by ~2×.
AI.motivation: To unlock cosmological information buried by non-linear structure formation and astrophysics, there is a need to recover the initial conditions of the Universe from late-time tracers, which would otherwise be inaccessible due to these complications.
AI.method: The approach uses a three-dimensional U-Net to reconstruct initial conditions from LIMFAST-simulated 21-cm and CO(1-0) line-intensity maps at z~8. Instrumental effects for SKA1-Low and COMAP-ERA-like surveys are modeled, including angular resolution and thermal noise. Performance is assessed via cross-correlation coefficients, and information gain is quantified through simulation-based inference of cosmological parameters from power-spectrum summaries complemented by Kullback-Leibler divergence diagnostics.
AI.result: Combining both tracers achieves |C(k)| ≥ 0.90 for k ≲ 0.75 Mpc⁻¹ in the noiseless case and |C(k)| ≥ 0.70 for k ≲ 0.3 Mpc⁻¹ with observational effects. Parameter constraints are tightened by the reconstruction, with uncertainties on σ₈ and n_s improving by ~2× in both noiseless and noisy settings, with smaller consistent gains for other parameters.
AI.conclusion: Joint analysis of future 21-cm and CO surveys combined with deep-learning-based reconstruction can partially recover otherwise inaccessible cosmological information from the late-time Universe.

title: KKR 18: A Late Arrival Galaxy?
comment: 12 pages, 13 figures. Submitted to The Astrophysical Journal
summary: KKR 18 is a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Void at a distance of 9.46 Mpc. It is gas rich and was experiencing vigorous star formation 20 - 100 Myr ago. Its metallicity is 4% of Solar from an emission spectrum, qualifying is as extremely metal poor (XMP). Its most remarkable characteristic is an extremely deficient Red Giant Branch. This feature is shared with a small number of other dwarf galaxies and it is inferred that they lack ancient stellar components. It is suggested that these are late arrival galaxies (LAG).

AI.tldr: KKR 18 is a dwarf irregular galaxy in the Local Void at 9.46 Mpc, gas-rich with vigorous star formation 20-100 Myr ago, extremely metal-poor (4% Solar), and notably lacking an ancient Red Giant Branch component—classifying it as a potential late arrival galaxy (LAG).
AI.motivation: The paper investigates KKR 18 as an example of extremely deficient Red Giant Branch dwarf galaxies, which are inferred to lack ancient stellar populations and may represent late arrival galaxies (LAGs) in the Local Void.
AI.method: The study characterizes KKR 18 through distance measurement (9.46 Mpc), gas content analysis, star formation history assessment (20-100 Myr ago), emission-spectrum metallicity determination (4% Solar), and examination of its Red Giant Branch population to infer the presence or absence of ancient stellar components.
AI.result: KKR 18 is confirmed as a gas-rich, extremely metal-poor (XMP) dwarf irregular galaxy with recent vigorous star formation and an extremely deficient Red Giant Branch, indicating it lacks ancient stellar components—a trait shared with a small number of other dwarf galaxies.
AI.conclusion: The deficient Red Giant Branch in KKR 18 and similar dwarf galaxies suggests they lack ancient stellar populations, leading to the inference that these systems are late arrival galaxies (LAGs) that began forming stars relatively recently.

title: Star Formation Evolution in Galaxy Pairs: Constraints from Morphological Disturbances and Recent Star Formation Histories
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures; accepted for publication in The Astrophysical Journal
summary: Galaxy interactions can enhance star formation, but how star formation evolves during galaxy interactions remains poorly constrained by observations. We combine pair separation, morphological disturbance, and recent star formation history to study this evolution. We measure morphological disturbance with the shape asymmetry parameter ($A_{\rm shape}$) using deep images from the DESI Legacy Surveys, and use Galaxy Zoo DESI classifications as an independent test. We infer recent star formation histories by comparing SFR and $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}α)$, which trace current star formation, with $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ and $D_n4000$, which are sensitive to stellar populations formed over longer timescales. At small projected separations, strongly disturbed galaxies show the strongest enhancements in SFR and $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}α)$, indicating that close encounters trigger strong star formation. At intermediate separations ($d_{\rm p}\sim100\,\mathrm{kpc}$), their current star formation is only moderately enhanced, but their $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ enhancement is the strongest. This indicates a larger contribution from intermediate-age stars formed during stronger star formation in the past $\sim0.1$--$1\,\mathrm{Gyr}$. The TNG100 analysis shows that this pattern results from rapid changes in SFR around close passage. SFR rises sharply during the encounter and declines as the galaxies move apart, while tidal disturbances remain visible. As short-lived massive stars disappear and intermediate-age A-type stars begin to dominate the spectrum, the $\mathrm{EW}(\mathrm{H}δ_A)$ enhancement peaks later than the SFR enhancement. Our results provide important observational evidence for the evolution of SFR along the merger sequence.

AI.tldr: This paper combines pair separation, morphological disturbance (using shape asymmetry parameter Ashape from DESI Legacy Surveys), and recent star formation history indicators to trace how star formation evolves during galaxy interactions and mergers.
AI.motivation: While galaxy interactions are known to enhance star formation, how star formation actually evolves as a function of merger stage/progression is poorly constrained by observations.
AI.method: The authors combine pair separation, morphological disturbance (shape asymmetry Ashape from DESI Legacy Surveys, with Galaxy Zoo DESI as a cross-check), and recent star formation histories inferred from SFR and EW(Hα) (current SF) versus EW(HδA) and Dn4000 (stellar populations over longer timescales). They also use TNG100 simulations to interpret the observed patterns.

At intermediate separations (~100 kpc), current SF is only moderately enhanced, but EW(HδA) enhancement peaks—indicating contributions from intermediate-age stars formed during stronger SF 0.1–1 Gyr earlier. TNG100 shows SFR rises sharply at close passage and declines as galaxies separate while tidal distortions persist, causing the HδA enhancement to peak later than the SFR peak.
AI.conclusion: The results provide important observational evidence for the evolution of star formation along the merger sequence, showing that SFR peaks at close passage and HδA-based signatures peak later as massive short-lived stars fade and intermediate-age A-type stars dominate the spectrum.

title: Membership Determination of 45 Open Clusters Beyond 3 kpc
comment: 14 pages, accepted for publication in Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Context. Open clusters (OCs) are fundamental tracers for studying the structure and chemical evolution of the Galactic disc. Reliable identification of cluster members, particularly at the faint end of the main sequence, remains challenging owing to severe field-star contamination and the declining photometric completeness for distant, obscured systems. Aims. We aim to identify and characterise distant OC candidates at heliocentric distances $d \gtrsim 3$ kpc using Gaia DR3 astrometry, with emphasis on improving the recovery of faint candidate members in highly contaminated stellar fields. Methods. We apply a probabilistic membership method based on Gaia DR3 proper motions and parallaxes. Candidate members are selected through combined astrometric criteria and refined via spatial filtering using radial density profiles, with photometric data serving as a consistency check. For clusters affected by significant extinction, near-infrared photometry from 2MASS is incorporated to compensate for the limitations of optical data. Results. We analyse a sample of 45 targets, comprising 30 previously reported OCs and 15 newly identified candidates, all located at $d \gtrsim 3$ kpc. The method yields more compact astrometric distributions and improves the recovery of faint candidate members in several systems. However, residual field contamination remains non-negligible for the most obscured clusters projected against the Galactic plane. Conclusions. Gaia DR3 astrometry provides an effective basis for the exploratory identification and first-order characterisation of distant OC candidates. Dedicated near-infrared follow-up observations will be essential for robust membership assessment in high extincted regions.

AI.motivation: Open clusters are fundamental tracers for studying the structure and chemical evolution of the Galactic disc, but reliable member identification—especially for faint stars in distant, obscured systems—remains difficult due to severe field-star contamination and declining photometric completeness.
AI.method: A probabilistic membership method based on Gaia DR3 proper motions and parallaxes is applied. Candidate members are selected via combined astrometric criteria, refined using radial density profile spatial filtering, and cross-checked with photometric data. title: Quantifying collision-driven mass loss in supermassive star formation: the role of stellar structure and accretion
summary: Observations of high-redshift galaxies with JWST have renewed interest in scenarios where supermassive stars form via runaway stellar collisions in dense clusters, yet the impact of collision-driven mass loss on their growth remains uncertain. In this work, we perform a post-processing analysis of 3D hydrodynamical simulations of the formation of a supermassive star, applying an analytic mass-loss prescription to stellar collisions while exploring different assumptions for the internal stellar structure. We consider a polytropic main-sequence model, a semi-analytic accreting protostar model, and structures derived from stellar evolution calculations. We find that the cumulative mass-loss fraction depends sensitively on the adopted stellar structure, ranging from $\lesssim 10-25\%$ for more compact configurations to $\gtrsim 30-40\%$ for more extended protostellar models. The importance of mass loss further depends on the dynamical state of the system, including the ratio of stellar velocity dispersion to the stellar surface escape velocity. We find significant uncertainty depending on the prescription used. As a result, collision-driven mass loss could significantly limit the growth of the central object, at least in some cases. Overall, our results indicate that uncertainties in the internal structure of rapidly accreting protostars represent a major source of systematic uncertainty and must be better constrained to robustly assess the viability of runaway-collision pathways for forming massive black hole seeds.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the impact of collision-driven mass loss on the formation of supermassive stars via runaway stellar collisions in dense clusters, using post-processing of 3D hydrodynamical simulations with different internal structure assumptions. Mass-loss fractions range widely (10-40%+) depending on structure, highlighting internal protostar structure as a major systematic uncertainty for massive black hole seed formation.
AI.motivation: JWST observations of high-redshift galaxies have renewed interest in supermassive star formation via runaway stellar collisions. However, the uncertain impact of collision-driven mass loss on stellar growth limits confidence in this pathway for forming massive black hole seeds.
AI.method: The authors perform post-processing analysis of 3D hydrodynamical simulations of supermassive star formation, applying an analytic mass-loss prescription to stellar collisions. They explore different internal structure assumptions: polytropic main-sequence models, semi-analytic accreting protostar models, and structures from stellar evolution calculations.
AI.result: Cumulative mass-loss fractions depend sensitively on stellar structure, ranging from less than 10-25% for compact configurations to more than 30-40% for extended protostellar models. Mass-loss importance also depends on the ratio of stellar velocity dispersion to surface escape velocity, with significant prescription-dependent uncertainty.

The internal structure of rapidly accreting protostars is a major source of systematic uncertainty that must be better constrained to robustly assess the viability of runaway-collision pathways for massive black hole seed formation.

title: Rubin J122659.4+090236: An Extremely Low Surface Brightness Galaxy Candidate Discovered in the Rubin LSST Early Data Preview 2
comment: 16 pages (including appendices), 9 figures, 4 tables
summary: We report the serendipitous discovery of an exceptionally low surface brightness galaxy (LSBG) candidate, Rubin J122659.4+090236, in Rubin Observatory imaging of the interacting NGC 4410 system, identified in the Cosmic Treasure Chest public release. 2D Sérsic modelling of the Rubin g, r, and i images reveals a nearly round system with a shallow profile (n ~ 0.4), an effective radius of R_e ~ 6'', and central surface brightnesses of $μ_{0,g}=27.52\pm0.04$, $μ_{0,r}=27.62\pm0.07$, and $μ_{0,i}=27.04\pm0.08$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$. These alternatives imply substantially different physical interpretations, ranging from a diffuse dwarf-like system to an exceptionally extended background LSBG. This discovery demonstrates Rubin's sensitivity to extremely diffuse galaxies and highlights the potential of the LSST survey to uncover large samples of such elusive systems across wide areas, enabling systematic studies of the LSBG population and its role in galaxy evolution.

AI.motivation: To demonstrate Rubin Observatory's sensitivity to extremely diffuse, low surface brightness galaxies and highlight the potential of the LSST survey to uncover large samples of such elusive systems for systematic study of the LSBG population and its role in galaxy evolution.
AI.method: The authors used 2D Sérsic modelling on Rubin g, r, and i images to characterize the galaxy's structural properties, and employed EAZY photometric redshift fitting—including a restricted fit over 0<z<0.1 without a redshift prior—to assess possible distance solutions.
AI.result: The galaxy has a nearly round morphology with a shallow Sérsic index (n~0.4), effective radius R_e~6'', and central surface brightnesses of ~27-27.6 mag arcsec^-2 in g, r, i bands. EAZY favours an intermediate-z solution (z~0.3), but a low-z solution (z~0.028) consistent with the NGC 4410 system is also permitted, implying interpretations ranging from a diffuse dwarf-like system to an exceptionally extended background LSBG.
AI.conclusion: Rubin Observatory imaging enables detection of extremely diffuse galaxies, and the LSST survey holds strong potential for discovering large samples of such elusive systems, enabling systematic studies of the LSBG population and its role in galaxy evolution.

title: Corona Australis 151: an extremely young protostar
comment: Accepted for publication in A&A Letters
summary:
Context. Prestellar cores are the birthplace of stars and planetary systems, but they are short-lived objects, since the initial stages of dense core evolution, collapse, and the formation of a protostellar seed are fast. In an effort to build a catalogue of bona-fide prestellar cores in the Solar neighbourhood, we used APEX observations to identify dynamically evolved cores among dense cores observed with Herschel. One of them, Corona Australis 151, stood out because of its centrally peaked structure, with densities above 1e7cm-3 in the central 500-1000 au, and high deuteration levels (N2D+/N2H+~0.5), suggestive of an evolved, prestellar stage.
  Aims. Corona Australis 151 appears to be an evolved prestellar core, but the presence of broad wings in some of the detected lines and a tentative 70micron detection with Herschel partially challenges its prestellar stage. We intend to assess its evolutionary stage.
  Methods. We analyse new ALMA data of the continuum emission and of several line tracers (including typical outflow tracers) at a resolution of~150-200au, tracing the envelope.
  Results. We unveil the presence of a compact and young outflow (projected dynamical age:~500yr), traced by SiO, CO, and H2CO emission. The continuum emission traces an envelope structure of size~1000 au and mass 0.33M_sun(assuming Tdust=20 K).
  Conclusions. Corona Australis 151 is an extremely young protostar, possibly one of the youngest known in the Solar neighbourhood, and hence a new laboratory to study the chemical and dynamical evolution at the dawn of star formation.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ALMA observations of Corona Australis 151, previously thought to be an evolved prestellar core, and reveals it is instead an extremely young protostar with a compact outflow (~500 yr dynamical age), an envelope of ~1000 au and 0.33 M_sun, making it one of the youngest protostars known in the Solar neighbourhood.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to determine the evolutionary stage of Corona Australis 151, which was initially classified as an evolved prestellar core based on its centrally peaked structure and high deuteration, but showed contradictory observational signatures (broad line wings and tentative 70 micron detection) that challenged its prestellar classification.
AI.method: The study uses new ALMA observations of continuum emission and multiple molecular line tracers (including typical outflow tracers such as SiO, CO, and H2CO) at ~150-200 au resolution to trace the envelope structure of Corona Australis 151.
AI.result: The observations reveal a compact and young outflow with a projected dynamical age of ~500 years, traced by SiO, CO, and H2CO emission. The continuum emission traces an envelope structure of ~1000 au in size with a mass of 0.33 M_sun (assuming T_dust = 20 K).
AI.conclusion: Corona Australis 151 is reclassified as an extremely young protostar, possibly one of the youngest known in the Solar neighbourhood, providing a new laboratory for studying chemical and dynamical evolution at the dawn of star formation.

title: PPN--spin degeneracies in mock S62-like stellar-orbit inference
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures
summary: We investigate the degeneracies between black hole (BH) spin effects and parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) parameters in the relativistic orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars orbiting Sagittarius A$^{\ast}$. Using a 1PN+SO Hamiltonian framework and synthetic astrometric and radial velocity datasets, we perform Bayesian parameter inference. For current baseline observational precisions, the dominant relativistic observable--the Schwarzschild periapsis advance--allows the recovery of the effective precession parameter $Υ$, while leaving the individual PPN parameters $γ$ and $β$ degenerate. Assuming microarcsecond-level astrometric precision, the spin-induced Lense-Thirring signal becomes partially detectable; fixing the PPN sector to General Relativity allows the BH spin magnitude to be constrained to an uncertainty of $\sim10^{-2}$. However, simultaneously varying PPN and spin parameters reveals a strong, approximately linear covariance between $Υ$ and the dimensionless spin parameter $χ$. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate that joint multi-star inference can disentangle the degeneracy by combining a wider-orbit star, which constrains the dominant 1PN sector, with a compact relativistic orbit that is sensitive to Lense-Thirring frame dragging.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the degeneracy between black hole spin effects and parametrized post-Newtonian (PPN) parameters in the orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars around Sagittarius A*. Using 1PN+SO Hamiltonian modeling and synthetic datasets, the authors find that spin and PPN parameters are strongly covariant, but joint multi-star inference can break this degeneracy by combining wide-orbit and compact relativistic orbit constraints.
AI.motivation: To understand the extent to which black hole spin effects and PPN parameters of alternative gravity theories can be disentangled using stellar orbital dynamics around the Galactic center supermassive black hole, particularly given the growing observational capabilities of instruments like GRAVITY.
AI.method: The study uses a 1PN+SO (first-order post-Newtonian plus spin-orbit) Hamiltonian framework to model the relativistic orbital dynamics of S2-like and S62-like stars. Synthetic astrometric and radial velocity datasets are generated and analyzed via Bayesian parameter inference under varying observational precision assumptions, including both current baseline precisions and future microarcsecond-level astrometry.
AI.result: At current precision levels, only the effective precession parameter Υ is recoverable while individual PPN parameters γ and β remain degenerate. With microarcsecond astrometry, the Lense-Thirring signal becomes partially detectable, allowing BH spin magnitude to be constrained to ~10⁻² uncertainty when PPN parameters are fixed to GR. However, simultaneous fitting reveals a strong approximately linear covariance between Υ and the dimensionless spin parameter χ. Joint multi-star inference using both a wider-orbit star and a compact relativistic orbit successfully disentangles this degeneracy.
AI.conclusion: A combined multi-star observational strategy—pairing wide-orbit stars that constrain the dominant 1PN sector with highly relativistic orbits sensitive to frame dragging—can effectively separate spin-induced precession from PPN parameter effects, thereby enabling unambiguous tests of GR around Sagittarius A*.

title: The dispersal law of young star clusters: free expansion -- A Gaia/eROSITA census of Orion and Sco--Cen
comment: Submitted to A&A. Comments are welcome
summary: We measure how young star clusters disperse over time in the two nearest star-forming complexes. Our sample comprises 44 \texttt{SigMA}-\textit{Gaia}-defined clusters in Orion and 31 in Sco--Cen, with isochronal ages of 2--25\,Myr. We extend each cluster's census with \textit{eROSITA}-selected young stars that share its parallax and motion and lie within the distance they could have traveled ballistically since birth. By 10--30\,Myr, about one in three former cluster stars lies outside the cluster's cataloged boundary. Across both complexes and the full age range, we find that (1) the half-member radius increases linearly with age, $\rfifty \simeq \sigbirth t$, (2) the velocity dispersion shows no measurable evolution, and (3) all studied clusters are unbound. These results support free expansion. Young clusters in Orion and Sco-Cen emerge unbound from their birth clouds and coast at their birth velocity dispersion without significant relaxation or a characteristic dispersal timescale. We further show that memberships defined by density contrast preferentially omit the fastest stars, making the same clusters appear to expand more slowly ($\propto t^{0.6}$), cool with age, and approach equilibrium.

AI.tldr: The study measures how young star clusters in Orion and Sco-Cen disperse over 2-25 Myr, finding that half-member radius grows linearly with age, velocity dispersion remains constant, and all clusters are unbound, supporting free expansion where clusters emerge unbound and coast outward without relaxation or a characteristic dispersal timescale.
AI.motivation: To determine how young star clusters disperse over time and to test whether their expansion is driven by free ballistic motion from unbound birth conditions, rather than relaxation-dominated processes.
AI.method: Analyzed 44 clusters in Orion and 31 in Sco-Cen (ages 2-25 Myr) defined via SigMA-Gaia, extending each cluster's census using eROSITA-selected young stars sharing parallax, motion, and lying within their ballistic travel distance since birth.
AI.result: By 10-30 Myr about one in three former cluster stars lies outside cataloged boundaries. Half-member radius increases linearly with age (r50 ~ sigma_birth * t), velocity dispersion shows no measurable evolution, and all studied clusters are unbound. Density-contrast-based memberships omit the fastest stars, producing artificially slower expansion (~t^0.6), apparent cooling, and apparent relaxation.
AI.conclusion: Young clusters in Orion and Sco-Cen emerge unbound from their birth clouds and freely coast at their birth velocity dispersion, without significant relaxation or a characteristic dispersal timescale. Selection effects in density-based membership methods create misleading impressions of slower expansion and quasi-equilibrium.

title: Stellar Population and Dynamical Modeling of Galaxies with Kinematically Misaligned Components: Age and Metallicity of Structural Components
comment: 31 pages, 16 figures, 4 tables
summary: We present stellar population and orbit modeling of two galaxies with kinematically misaligned components, PGC 35706 and LEDA 2220522, extending previous Schwarzschild dynamical models. Using spatially resolved age and metallicity maps from NBursts full spectral fitting of MaNGA data with the E-MILES grid, we solve a regularized bounded linear inverse problem that assigns light-weighted SSP-equivalent age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells in the $(R,λ_z)$ plane. Component means and radial profiles use projected mass within the actual MaNGA field of view; profile segments with local component fractions below $1\%$ are treated as weakly constrained. In LEDA 2220522, the counter-rotating disk is younger than the co-rotating disk, $1.32\pm0.04$ versus $1.61\pm0.06$ Gyr, and more metal-rich, $[\mathrm{M/H}]=-0.450\pm0.043$ versus $-0.613\pm0.024$. Its rotation agrees with that of the H$α$ ionized gas, supporting late supply of chemically enriched retrograde gas without requiring multiple accretion episodes with alternating angular momentum. In PGC 35706, the counter-rotating disk contains $8.8\%$ of the mass in the observed field and is formally older than the co-rotating disk by $1.36\pm0.51$ Gyr and more metal-poor by $0.130\pm0.046$ dex. These differences are preliminary because the projected data provide limited support. Fifty Monte Carlo realizations confirm stability of the projected maps against statistical noise, but not uniqueness in individual phase-space cells. The stellar population and orbit approach is therefore applicable to MaNGA data when local projected component fractions and systematics from regularization and the dynamical model are explicitly considered.

AI.tldr: The paper presents stellar population and orbit modeling of two galaxies (PGC 35706 and LEDA 2220522) with kinematically misaligned components, extending Schwarzschild dynamical models by assigning light-weighted SSP-equivalent age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells via a regularized bounded linear inverse problem. Key findings include a younger, more metal-rich counter-rotating disk in LEDA 2220522 (consistent with late retrograde gas accretion), and an older, more metal-poor counter-rotating disk in PGC 35706 (preliminary results). Monte Carlo realizations confirm map stability but not uniqueness in individual cells.
AI.motivation: To extend Schwarzschild dynamical models by incorporating stellar population properties (age, metallicity) into orbital cells, enabling decomposition of kinematically misaligned (e.g., counter-rotating) components and testing formation scenarios such as gas accretion events versus multiple accretion episodes.
AI.method: The authors use spatially resolved age and metallicity maps from NBursts full spectral fitting of MaNGA data with the E-MILES stellar population grid. They solve a regularized bounded linear inverse problem that assigns light-weighted SSP-equivalent age, metallicity, and mass-to-light ratio to orbital cells in the (R, λ_z) plane from Schwarzschild dynamical models. Component means and radial profiles are computed using projected mass within the MaNGA field of view, treating cells with local component fractions below 1% as weakly constrained. Fifty Monte Carlo realizations are used to assess stability against statistical noise.
AI.result: In LEDA 2220522, the counter-rotating disk is younger (1.32±0.04 vs 1.61±0.06 Gyr) and more metal-rich ([M/H]=-0.450±0.043 vs -0.613±0.024) than the co-rotating disk, with rotation matching the Hα ionized gas, supporting late supply of chemically enriched retrograde gas. In PGC 35706, the counter-rotating disk contains 8.8% of the mass and is formally older by 1.36±0.51 Gyr and more metal-poor by 0.130±0.046 dex, though these are preliminary due to limited projected data support. Monte Carlo tests confirm stability of projected maps against noise but not uniqueness of individual phase-space cells.
AI.conclusion: The stellar population and orbit approach is applicable to MaNGA data, but requires explicit consideration of local projected component fractions and systematics from regularization and the dynamical model when interpreting results on kinematically misaligned galaxy components.

title: Rapid quenching and early gas depletion in the core of a galaxy protocluster at z=2.2
comment: 16 pages (of which 2 pages for Appendices), 9 Figures, 4 Tables. A&A in press
summary: Understanding how galaxy evolution is affected in forming high-z overdensities is a major open question in modern astrophysics. Here, we present the average properties of the quiescent galaxy population recently identified in the core of the Spiderweb protocluster at z = 2.16. By stacking observations from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST; F160W imaging and G141 grism spectroscopy), the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST; PaBeta narrowband imaging), and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA; 1.2 mm dust continuum imaging), we constrained their ensemble star formation history (SFH), residual dust-obscured star formation, and cold gas mass, respectively. The inferred average SFH indicates steady stellar mass growth, with progenitor SFRs consistent with those of massive Halpha emitters (HAEs) in the same structure. This is followed by rapid quenching, on average 500 Myr prior to observation. No significant age differences are found between active galactic nucleus (AGN) hosts and non-AGN systems. We find weak PaBeta emission for 80% of the sample, yet with dust-obscured star formation rates consistent with quiescence in all but one source (ID 443) excluded from the sample. Our galaxies remain individually and globally undetected in the dust continuum, yielding an average gas fraction fgas= Mmol/Mstar<7%, consistent with previously reported gas depletion trends with stellar mass observed in neighboring HAEs. We thus find the Spiderweb protocluster to host a sizable population of gas-depleted, massive quenched galaxies in its core, likely descending from main-sequence galaxy progenitors and building the first elements of the red sequence in this high-z forming cluster.

The galaxies have steady stellar mass growth from progenitors similar to massive Hα emitters, followed by rapid quenching ~500 Myr before observation. They show weak Paβ emission, are individually and globally undetected in 1.2 mm dust continuum, and have gas fractions below 7%, indicating gas-depleted, massive quenched galaxies building the first elements of the red sequence.

Galaxies remain undetected in dust continuum, with average gas fraction <7%, consistent with gas depletion trends observed in neighboring HAEs.
AI.conclusion: The Spiderweb protocluster hosts a sizable population of gas-depleted, massive quenched galaxies in its core, likely descending from main-sequence progenitors and building the first elements of the red sequence in this high-z forming cluster.
